extracted.intended_audience: students and general readers of natural philosophy / physics
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition of fundamental principles governing the direction and rhythmic character of motion across physical, geological, astronomical, meteorological, and biological domains. The chapter gives axiomatic statements (e.g., persistence of force), derivations (composition of forces), and extensive illustrative examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition of forces / resultant representation
rubrics_metrics.description: By what is known among mathematicians as the composition of forces, there may be found for any two of these, a single force of such amount and direction as to produce on the body an exactly equal effect. ... the diagonal of this parallelogram represents the amount and direction of a force that is equivalent to the two.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains the parallelogram construction: draw straight lines proportional to force magnitudes in their directions, complete the parallelogram, the diagonal gives the resultant. Repeat pairwise to reduce many forces to two. Examples and stepwise reduction provided; used as basis for deducing motion direction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motion follows the line of greatest traction / least resistance / resultant
rubrics_metrics.description: Thus the law that motion follows the line of greatest traction, or the line of least resistance, or the resultant of the two, is a necessary deduction from that primordial truth which transcends proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If opposing resultants are equal and opposite, no motion; if unequal, motion occurs in direction of greater or of the resultant. Illustrated by suspended weights, men pulling, and general arrays of forces. Presented as a necessary (not merely empirical) law derived from persistence of force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Persistence of force (primordial datum)
rubrics_metrics.description: The consciousness that this residuary force cannot disappear, but must manifest itself in some equivalent change — the consciousness that force is persistent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treated as the ultimate datum from which directional laws are deduced; used to reject assertions that a force can be expended without effect. Serves as foundational axiom underpinning composition of forces and conclusions about motion direction and continuation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Residual (unneutralized) force produces motion in its direction
rubrics_metrics.description: This residuary force that is not neutralized by an opposing one, must move the body in the direction in which it is acting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applied to paired examples (weights over a pulley, rival pullers): the one producing motion in its own direction is judged greater. The text notes that our evidence of excess force is the motion produced, making the statement tautological but grounded in persistence of force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inertia / motion continues when unopposed (mechanical axiom)
rubrics_metrics.description: The mechanical axiom that, if left to itself, matter moving in any direction will continue in that direction with undiminished velocity, is but an indirect assertion of the persistence of force.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explained as a corollary of persistence of force: the force manifested in transfer along a line cannot disappear without producing some equal manifestation, which absent conflict must be further transfer. Examples include motion in vacuum and continuation of trajectories absent external interference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motion as cause of subsequent motion along same line
rubrics_metrics.description: Motion once set up along any line, becomes itself a cause of subsequent motion along that line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to justify continued transfer and propagation of motion (e.g., impulses through matter, waves); supports idea that an initial motion propagates unless dissipated or transformed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transformation and dissipation of motion in media (friction, heat, structural change)
rubrics_metrics.description: A liquid that follows a certain channel ... loses part of its motion in the shape of heat, through friction and collision with the matter forming its bed. ... in the conducting power of metals, the conducting power is for the time decreased by the heat which the passage of electricity itself generates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describes mechanisms by which motion is transformed (into heat, chemical change, structural rearrangement) and how such transformations reduce available motion. Examples: river cutting its bed, electricity heating conductors, nervous discharge subject to chemical changes. Also notes that structural modification can reduce subsequent resistance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical modification reduces subsequent obstruction (path-dependence)
rubrics_metrics.description: As much of this remaining motion as is taken up in changing the positions of the units, must leave these by so much less able to obstruct subsequent motion in the same direction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains how previous transfers that alter structure (e.g., erosion by flowing water) make future motion along that path easier; illustrated by river-course cutting and reduced resistance after initial motion.

rubrics_metrics.name: All motion is rhythmical when forces are unbalanced
rubrics_metrics.description: "Wherever we see motion, its direction must be that of the greatest force." ... From the ensemble of the facts ... it will be seen that rhythm results wherever there is a conflict of forces not in equilibrium.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues rhythm (oscillation, undulation, vibration) is ubiquitous: from pennant fluttering, sail flapping, ripples, waves, to etherial undulations (light, heat) and electric discharge. Where antagonistic forces exist without equilibrium, uniform motion is impossible and rhythm emerges as the unavoidable alternative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rhythms are generally compound (primary and secondary rhythms; beats; interference)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rhythm is very generally not simple but compound. There are usually at work various forces, causing undulations differing in rapidity; and hence it continually happens that besides the primary rhythms there are secondary rhythms, produced by the periodic coincidence and antagonism of the primary ones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains beats in acoustics, interference in light, tidal fortnightly modulation (solar and lunar), and superposition of waves on the sea as examples. Compound rhythms produce double, triple, etc., orders and complex temporal patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apparent exceptions are due to interruption; underlying rhythms would persist
rubrics_metrics.description: Should it be said that at any rate there are some motions, as those of projectiles, which are not rhythmical, the reply is, that the exception is apparent only; and that these motions would be rhythmical if they were not interrupted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uses cannonball trajectory: without arrest by Earth's substance, it would describe an eccentric ellipse and return, hence rhythm. The cannon's explosion itself produces atmospheric undulations; shock produces vibrations in bodies struck.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rhythms are necessarily incomplete and non-perfectly periodic
rubrics_metrics.description: A secondary conclusion must not be omitted. ... rhythm is necessarily incomplete. A truly rectilinear rhythm can arise only when the opposing forces are in exactly the same line; ... All other proportions and directions of the two forces will produce an ellipse of greater or less eccentricity. And when ... above two forces are engaged, the curve described must be more complex; and cannot exactly repeat itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues that perfect rectilinear or circular rhythms require infinitely improbable precise alignments and ratios; usual outcomes are ellipses or complex non-repeating oscillations. Greater numbers of interacting forces increase irregularity; regularity declines with system complexity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scale-invariant occurrence of rhythms across domains
rubrics_metrics.description: Thus in all the changes ... by the Solar System; ... in all processes of organic development and function; ... and in all modifications of structure and activity in societies; the implied movements are of necessity determined in the manner above set forth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides cross-domain examples: spiral nebulae and double stars (astronomical), planetary periodicities, tidal modulation, meteorological cycles, geological strata and volcanic/earthquake intermittency, biological rhythms (heart, digestion, sleep), and social rhythms. Demonstrates universality and compound nesting of rhythms (e.g., quadruple rhythm of Earth's light/heat cycles).

rubrics_metrics.name: Meteorological and terrestrial rhythms driven by solar heating cycles and local interactions
rubrics_metrics.description: Those terrestrial processes whose dependence on the solar heat is direct, of course exhibit a rhythm that corresponds to the periodically changing amount of heat which each part of the Earth receives. ... During wet weather ... the tendency to condense ... does not show itself in continuous rain; but the period is made up of rainy days and days that are wholly or partially fair.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Details mechanisms: diurnal/annual/decennial magnetic variations, oceanic and atmospheric currents varying with seasons, monsoons, evaporation/condensation alternations, mountain-induced cycles. Links meteorological rhythms to resulting sedimentary and geological periodic signatures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Biological (organic) rhythms: nested periodicities of function
rubrics_metrics.description: Perhaps nowhere are the illustrations of rhythm so numerous and so manifest as among the phenomena of life. ... The swallowing of food is effected by a wave ... the blood ... is propelled not in a uniform current but in pulses; and it is aerated by lungs that alternately contract and expand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enumerates primary rhythms (peristalsis, heart pulses, respiration, ciliary vibration) compounded with longer cycles (feeding/rest cycles, sleep) and still slower rises and falls of functional activity. Emphasizes nested, compound rhythmic organization in organisms.
